newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani tribal elders block women from voting.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani tribal elders block women from voting.

text.p: Moslem tribal elders in a Pakistani border region stopped women from voting in Monday's election, saying such behaviour violated Islamic modesty.

"Voting by women is un-Islamic and is also against our traditions," said Maulana Abdul Hadi, a Moslem cleric in the tribal areas near Afghanistan, where people are voting under universal adult suffrage for the first time.

Hadi, who heads the religious Tanzim Ittehad Ulema-i-Qabail organisation, said a National Assembly (lower house) candidate in the Khyber Agency had defied a tribal ruling against letting women vote by bringing them to polling stations.
He said a tribal jirga, or council, would decide on a suitable punishment. Last month Khyber Agency elders decided to burn the house of anyone who allowed women to vote.

Sixteen of a total of 700 registered women voters had cast their ballots at one Khyber Agency polling station and 90 out of 900 at another when tribal elders intervened, broadcasting warnings from a mosque loudspeaker in Jamrud.
Representatives of a national Aurat (Woman) Foundation and the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan failed to persuade the elders to change their minds.
Local officials said they expected women voters to fare better in two other tribal areas, South Waziristan and Kurram Agencies.
In South Waziristan, inhabited by warlike Mahsud tribes, women's voting has been encouraged by a local youth organisation and Kurram's Shi'ite Moslem population is relatively liberal.
Witnesses said voter turnout in general was fairly high in the semi-autonomous Federally Administered Tribal Areas, home to an estimated 3.4 million tribespeople.

Political parties are banned in the region, which has enjoyed a special status since Britain's Sir Mortimer Durand drew the so-called Durand Line to demarcate the frontier between British India and Afghanistan in 1880-84.
